START HERE

You have the biology.
We'll teach you the tools.

Start with orientation and basic computer concepts, then choose a language and research route that fit your work. These are suggested branches, not a mandatory course or a promise of a complete analysis pipeline.

Start with orientation → See the learning path ↓

WHO THIS IS FOR

Is this for me?

You do not need to arrive with code or software experience. You only need a biological question worth investigating.

THE FOUNDATION

Choose a comfortable entry point, then follow the relevant prerequisites.

The four cards move from orientation through basic computing to a shell and software environments. Each lesson states its format and prerequisites; biological data formats are an optional reference, not a required stop. HPC is a separate optional track below.

01

Orient to bioinformatics

See how biological questions, data, tools, and interpretation fit together.

Start → 02

Understand computers and files

Build a mental model of files, folders, formats, and computing before using a shell.

Start → 03

Practice the command line

Start with safe navigation; continue through Parts 2 and 3 only as you need those skills.

Start → 04

Manage software environments

Practice isolating software before choosing one programming-language route.

Start →

Choose R or Python

Pick the language that suits your tools, collaborators, and analysis. You do not need to learn both before continuing; either route joins the shared statistics and study-design foundations.

Learn R and Tidyverse · Learn Python

Optional: use HPC

A cluster is not a universal entrance requirement. If your institution provides access or your workload needs it, start with connection and follow the Slurm lessons; follow local policies.

Open the optional HPC track

Use references when needed

Look up biological file formats when a particular input is unfamiliar; it is not a prerequisite before learning shell basics.

Open the data-formats reference
💡 Tip: Work slowly enough to actually understand what each command does. Don't just copy and paste!

CHOOSE YOUR ROUTE

Pick your specialization.

Once you've built the foundation, choose the topic that matches your research. These routes are starting points into related guides, labs, and templates, not complete end-to-end research pipelines.

ROUTE 01

Single-Cell & Spatial Omics

Start with scRNA-seq basics and cell-level QC, then annotation. Integration, multimodal analysis, and trajectory methods are optional branches for suitable inputs and questions.

Start with scRNA-seq →
ROUTE 02

Genomics & Variants

Call variants from whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, annotate mutations, and explore long-read data.

Start with WES →
ROUTE 03

Microbial Omics

Profile microbial communities, assemble metagenomes, and discover functional pathways in your samples.

Start with 16S rRNA →
ROUTE 04

Evolutionary Genomics

Build phylogenies, identify orthologs, and explore genome-scale evolutionary relationships.

Start with Phylogeny →

ROADMAP & REQUIREMENTS

Prerequisites, Setup & Learning Outcomes

Use these general setup pointers and practice checkpoints alongside the requirements of your chosen lesson. Software, input files, and computing needs vary by exercise and dataset.

01

Hardware Requirements

Many small foundation exercises can be attempted on a modern laptop. Check the chosen lesson's operating-system and memory requirements; needed resources depend on the tools and input size.

Larger analyses may need HPC or other high-memory computing. Estimate memory, storage, threads, and runtime for the actual data and tools; follow your institution's scheduler policies.
02

Software Stack

Use the versions and dependencies specified by the chosen lesson or its tool documentation. The collection is not standardized on one Python or R version. Record your environment and check compatibility before running examples.

  • Package Managers: Mamba / Micromamba (faster than default Conda)
  • Core Languages: Python (Scanpy, Biopython), R (Seurat, DESeq2)
  • Orchestration: Snakemake, Nextflow, Docker & Singularity
03

Expected Outcomes

With practice, this curriculum can help wet-lab researchers progress from copying code snippets toward planning, adapting, and checking reproducible analysis pipelines.

Practice milestone: complete the Command-Line Part 1 lab. Expected result: a disposable project tree with the named zero-byte placeholder files, safe copy/move checks, and an explicit finding that the placeholders are not sequencing data. Feedback: inspect the displayed paths and file sizes; the lesson explains both what each output confirms and what it cannot establish. Templates and exercises do not by themselves produce research findings.

Estimated Study Order & Specialization Tracks

Track A: Transition

Wet-Lab to Dry-Lab Analyst

A suggested foundation route. After environments, choose either R or Python; both choices meet again at statistics and study design.

  1. Introduction to Bioinformatics
  2. Computer and Data Fundamentals
  3. Command Line Part 1 → Part 2 → Part 3
  4. Micromamba environments; then choose R or Python
  5. Statistics → Experimental design and batch effects
  6. Pseudobulk Differential Expression for scRNA-seq (only for suitable replicated designs; not bulk RNA-seq)
Track B: Single-Cell

Single-Cell & Spatial Specialist

A branched route: basic scRNA-seq and cell-level QC precede annotation. Integrate only if dataset structure and the question warrant it; assess integration separately from basic QC.

  1. scRNA-seq Basics → cell-level QC fundamentals
  2. Cell-type annotation methods
  3. Optional when needed: integration strategies → integration metrics (LISI/silhouette; advanced)
  4. Choose question-led follow-up: downstream analysis, communication, or optional trajectory for a plausible continuous process
  5. Spatial and multimodal methods are separate options: spatial · CITE-seq/WNN
Track C: Genomics

Reference-aware variant analysis

Prepare with data quality and reference context. WES is an assay-specific branch; it does not lead into scRNA-seq by default. HPC and workflow tools are optional computing choices.

  1. Quality-control fundamentals and data formats reference as needed
  2. Reference genomes and annotation
  3. Whole Exome Sequencing variant calling
  4. Optional computing support: HPC · workflow automation · containers

Optional track: HPC and scalable computing

Cluster access is not required to start or to follow the analysis routes above. If you have authorized access and a workload that needs it, follow Connecting to HPC → Slurm basics → job scripts. Consult HPC support when needed. Follow your institution's security and scheduler policies.

Dr. Abbasi's Advice: How to Assess Your Progress

When students in our lab at the Bordeaux Institute of Oncology (BRIC INSERM) begin computational research, I always emphasize that true mastery is not memorizing syntax, it is understanding your data and knowing how to troubleshoot when something breaks. Ask yourself these three checkpoint questions as you move through our modules:

Checkpoint 1: Environment Integrity

Can you recreate an environment from a specification, record software versions, run a small check, and document any platform or dependency differences?

Checkpoint 2: Resource Allocation

Can you use a small test run and job logs to estimate walltime, threads, and memory, then revise resource requests according to your cluster's policies?

Checkpoint 3: Biological Interpretation

Can you interpret relevant QC plots, explain the biological and statistical reasons for a filtering choice, and identify what further checks are needed?

Already comfortable with the basics?

If you already know the basics, choose a question-led route or use the full catalogue. HPC knowledge is not required to browse or begin. Check each page’s learning-format label: some are guided labs; others explain concepts, provide adaptable templates, or serve as references.

Start at 01. Select a step to preview its lesson.

  1. 01The big pictureFrom a question to an analysis plan→
  2. 02Terminal navigationKnow where you are and how to move→

LATER, WHEN YOU NEED IT

Follow your biological question.

These are optional routes, not extra prerequisites. Open the topic that fits your data.

Single-cell RNA sequencing

Start with scRNA-seq basics, then cell-level quality control, then cell-type annotation. QC comes before annotation.

Integration and advanced LISI/silhouette metrics are optional and are not substitutes for basic QC. Follow a suitable question to downstream analysis, cell-cell communication, or trajectory inference for a plausible continuous process. Spatial and CITE-seq are separate options.

Pseudobulk differential expression requires replicated single-cell samples and an appropriate design; it is not a bulk RNA-seq tutorial.

DNA sequencing and variants

For whole-exome sequencing (WES), consult quality-control fundamentals and the data-formats reference as needed, then read reference genomes and annotation before the WES variant-calling template. WES is assay-specific and is not the default route into single-cell analysis.

Microbial sequence analysis

Explore 16S profiling and Prokka genome annotation; check that lesson for the relevant inputs and scope before beginning.

Evolution and phylogeny

Review reference genomes and annotation as appropriate before using the evolutionary phylogeny template.

Tools and references

Install project software only when a lesson needs it. You do not need a cluster to begin.

Software setup and practical references

Micromamba environments isolate a project's software. You need terminal comfort and permission to install packages. The collection is not standardized on one Python or R version; follow each lesson's dependencies.

Continue to command-line Part 2 or Part 3 when needed. In Part 1, zero-byte placeholder files are not sequencing data.

Look up data formats, statistics for independent two-group comparisons, or study design and batch effects as needed. Workflow automation and containers are optional.

HPC and cluster computing (optional)

HPC requires authorized institutional access. Follow local security and scheduler policies. If your project needs a cluster, see connecting to HPC, Slurm basics, job scripts, and HPC support.

Suggested routes, not a required course or a complete analysis pipeline. Lessons include guides, labs, templates, and references.
